query: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but very poor room-temperature ductility, while its irradiation resistance has primarily been proposed by first-principles calculations. What intervention could improve its room-temperature ductility without compromising its high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline under room-temperature, 1600 °C, and irradiation assessments, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a falsification experiment.

generation.conditions: Room temperature to 1600 °C, irradiation dose up to 10 dpa
generation.mechanism: Grain boundary segregation reduces grain boundary cohesion and promotes dislocation mobility, enhancing room-temperature ductility
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved room-temperature ductility by 20% relative to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline, maintained mechanical performance at 1600 °C, and maintained irradiation resistance
generation.boundary: Temperature range: room temperature to 1600 °C, irradiation dose: up to 10 dpa
generation.uncertainty: The exact amount of grain boundary segregation required to achieve improved ductility is uncertain, and the potential effects of segregation on high-temperature mechanical performance and irradiation resistance need further investigation

falsification_experiment.design: Compare room-temperature ductility of grain boundary segregated and non-segregated NbMoTaW
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the room-temperature ductility of the grain boundary segregated sample is not improved by at least 15% relative to the non-segregated sample, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: As we all know, the alloying of metals with certain specific elements can very effectively improve alloy properties through various strengthening methods such as precipitation strengthening, solution strengthening, and interface strengthening [,,,]. Hf is an essential alloying element for both the interface strengthening of superalloys and the strengthening of the Ni-Al B2 phase [,,,,,]. Recently, some studies have shown that adding a small amount of Hf to a single-phase FCC high-entropy alloy could improve the room-temperature mechanical property of the alloy without significantly reducing the ductility of the alloy through the precipitation of intermetallic compounds such as Ni7Hf2 and Laves phases [,]. However, these studies mainly focus on single-phase high-entropy alloys, and the addition of Hf is relatively large, usually more than one atom. Therefore, the effect of trace Hf addition on the properties of the alloy at room temperature and high temperature is worthy of in-depth investigation.

One such class comprises the RHEAs which, because of their high melting points, have been proposed as candidates for ultrahigh-temperature applications. However, a single-phase RHEA, TiZrHfNbTa, was recently shown to be significantly weaker in creep than CMSX-4 despite the former’s higher melting point. The weakness was ascribed to two factors: faster diffusion in the BCC matrix of the RHEA relative to the FCC matrix of CMSX-4 and a lack of precipitates. Additional research is therefore needed to enhance the creep strength of TiZrHfNbTa, for example, by the introduction of suitable strengthening precipitates. Meanwhile, RHEAs with higher melting points must also be investigated since diffusion will be slower in such materials. One such RHEA is VNbMoTaW, whose melting point is ~500 °C higher than TiZrHfNbTa,,. However, it has a major disadvantage: lack of ductility at room temperature even in compression. In contrast, TiZrHfNbTa exhibits ductility at room temperature both in compression and in tension (~8%), albeit not as much as the highly ductile and fracture-resistant FCC HEAs. Typically, refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs), comprising a two-phase ordered B2 + BCC microstructure, exhibit extraordinarily high yield strengths, but poor ductility at room temperature, limiting their engineering application. The poor ductility is attributed to the continuous matrix being the ordered B2 phase in these alloys. This paper presents a novel approach to microstructural engineering of RHEAs to form an “inverted” BCC + B2 microstructure with discrete B2 precipitates dispersed within a continuous BCC matrix, resulting in improved room temperature compressive ductility, while maintaining high yield strength at both room and elevated temperature.
